topic: How the sailing stones of Death Valley move
hook: In a dry lake in Death Valley, rocks move on their own.

scenes.narration: The lake bed is called Racetrack Playa. Scattered across its flat, cracked surface are heavy stones. Behind each one runs a long, winding track, carved into the dried mud.
Some of these stones weigh more than 300 kilograms. Yet for most of a century, nobody had ever actually watched one move.
For decades, people guessed. Powerful winds. Mysterious magnetic fields. Even mischievous pranksters, sneaking out at night.
In 2013, a team of scientists set up time-lapse cameras and weather stations on the playa, and patiently waited.
That winter, they finally saw it happen. A thin sheet of ice formed on a shallow, temporary pond. Then the morning sun broke it into enormous floating panels.
Light wind pushed the ice, and the ice pushed the stones. They crept along at two to five metres a minute.
No aliens. No magnets. Just ice, wind and incredible patience.

loop_line: So next time you see a rock in the desert, look closely. It may be waiting for winter, ready to move on its own.
title: The sailing stones of Death Valley, solved
